chunks: I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Ridha (peace be upon him): 'Was God, Mighty and Majestic, aware of Himself before He created the creation?' He said: 'Yes.'

I said: 'Did He see it (His Self) and hear it?' He said: 'He was not in need of that, because He did not happen to ask it nor seek from it. He is His Self, and His Self is He. His Power is pervading. Thus, He is not in need of naming Himself.'

But He chose names for others to call Him by, because when He is not called by His Name, He would not be recognized. Thus, the first of what He chose for Himself was al-Ali al-Azim (the Exalted, the Magnificent), because He is loftier than all things. So its meaning is Allah, and His Name is al-Ali al-Azim — it is the first of His Names. He is Exalted above every thing.

key_terms.الْعَلِيُّ الْعَظِيمُ: Al-Ali al-Azim — the Exalted, the Magnificent: the first divine Name, expressing absolute transcendence
key_terms.عَارِفاً بِنَفْسِهِ: Self-knowledge of God — divine self-awareness that is not dependent on sensory faculties
key_terms.قُدْرَتُهُ نَافِذَةٌ: His Power is pervading — divine omnipotence that encompasses all things without external instruments
key_terms.هُوَ نَفْسُهُ وَنَفْسُهُ هُوَ: He is His Self and His Self is He — absolute divine simplicity and self-identity

ai.seo_question: Did God know Himself before creating the world according to Imam al-Ridha?
ai.summary: In this profound theological dialogue, Ibn Sinan asks Imam al-Ridha (a.s.) whether God possessed self-knowledge before creation, and the Imam confirms this while explaining that God's knowing Himself transcends the creaturely modalities of seeing and hearing. The Imam articulates a sophisticated doctrine: God did not need sensory faculties to know Himself because He is absolutely identical with His Self and His Power is all-pervading. The divine Names were chosen not for God's own benefit but as a concession to creation, enabling creatures to recognize and call upon the Divine — the first such Name being al-Ali al-Azim (the Exalted, the Magnificent), reflecting God's absolute transcendence above all created things.
